C005.subject: Within-industry labor mobility across local labor markets
C005.object: industry-level and individual-level estimates of employer concentration's effect on net earnings gains from minimum wage increases
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Within-industry labor mobility across local labor markets industry-level and individual-level estimates of employer concentration's effect on net earnings gains from minimum wage increases]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal employer-employee matched data (e.g., LEHD) to track individual workers' earnings and mobility across local labor markets within the same industry before and after minimum wage increases, then compare industry-level concentration measures (e.g., HHI) with individual-level earnings gains. — This directly tests whether within-industry labor mobility across markets alters the relationship between employer concentration and net earnings gains from minimum wage hikes, by contrasting aggregated industry estimates with individual-level outcomes.

[PATH:theoretical] Simulation or structural model of spatial equilibrium with heterogeneous firms and worker mobility costs, calibrated to US data (2000-2020), to examine how within-industry cross-market mobility affects the divergence between industry-level and individual-level estimates of concentration's effect on minimum wage pass-through. — A theoretical model can isolate the causal mechanism by which mobility amplifies divergence, providing predictions that can be tested against empirical patterns.

[PATH:literature] Literature review of studies on minimum wage effects on earnings, employer concentration, and labor mobility, focusing on papers that estimate both industry-level and individual-level effects (e.g., Azar et al., 2020; Dube et al., 2020; Rinz, 2022). — Synthesizing existing evidence can reveal whether the hypothesized divergence is consistently observed across different data sets and methodologies, and identify gaps in current knowledge.

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal employer-employee matched panel data (e.g., LEHD data for U.S. states) tracking industry-level labor mobility rates and individual-level earnings changes after minimum wage increases — Directly tests whether higher industry-level mobility (e.g., worker flows between firms) widens the gap between aggregated industry estimates and individual-level estimates of employer concentration's effect on net earnings gains from minimum wage hikes.

[PATH:theoretical] Simulation studies or structural models of labor markets with heterogeneous firms and worker sorting, calibrated to U.S. data 2000-2020 — Allows controlled variation of industry-level labor mobility parameters to isolate how aggregation bias in concentration measures translates into discrepancy between industry and individual-level earnings effect estimates.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing empirical studies on minimum wage impacts and employer concentration, focusing on studies that report both industry-level and individual-level estimates — Synthesizes available evidence to see if the hypothesized discrepancy pattern consistently appears across different contexts and data sources, and whether mobility measures are a common moderator.

[PATH:empirical] Linked employer-employee panel data from a country with high union density variation (e.g., Germany or Sweden), merged with firm-level union density records and minimum wage variation across industries and over time. — Allows estimation of how firm-specific union density moderates the relationship between employer concentration and net earnings gains from minimum wage increases, testing whether the sign of the divergence reverses above the 15% threshold under high rents.

[PATH:theoretical] Bargaining theory models with heterogeneous firms and unions (e.g., extensions of the right-to-manage or efficient bargaining framework) that incorporate employer concentration and minimum wage pass-through. — Can derive predictions about when and why firm-level union density might reverse the sign of the divergence between industry-level and individual-level estimates, providing formal conditions to test empirically.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis or systematic review of existing studies on minimum wage effects, union density, and employer concentration, focusing on studies that report both industry-level and individual-level estimates. — Synthesizes available evidence to identify patterns consistent with the reversal hypothesis, and highlights gaps where new empirical work is needed.

qualifier.condition: when firm-specific union density exceeds 15% and firm-specific rents are high

[PATH:empirical] Matched employer-employee panel data from the U.S. Census Bureau's Longitudinal Employer-Household Dynamics (LEHD) program, linked with firm-level concentration measures and minimum wage changes at state/county level — This data would allow direct estimation of how firm-level worker bargaining power (e.g., union presence, turnover costs, rent-sharing) moderates the gap between industry-level and individual-level effects of employer concentration on earnings gains from minimum wage increases.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical model of bargaining under oligopsony with heterogeneous worker bargaining power, building on Manning (2003) and Card, Cardoso & Kline (2016) — A formal model can clarify the mechanisms through which firm-level bargaining power alters the pass-through of minimum wage shocks to individual earnings, and predict conditions under which industry-level estimates diverge from individual-level ones.

[PATH:literature] Literature review of empirical studies on minimum wage effects under varying labor market concentration (e.g., Azar et al. 2019, Rinz 2022, Berger et al. 2022) with meta-analysis focusing on bargaining power proxies — Systematic synthesis of existing evidence can reveal whether the divergence between aggregation levels is consistently moderated by firm-level bargaining power, and identify gaps in current empirical designs.

[PATH:theoretical] Structural labor market models incorporating search frictions, firm concentration, and collective bargaining — Models can simulate how industry-level mobility constraints and bargaining power interact with minimum wage changes to predict whether concentration effects are magnified or dampened, providing a formal test of the amplification mechanism.
